> **Design preview.** These examples describe the proposed API in
> `docs/api-vision.md`. They are non-executable and have not been run.
> Real-client examples would require credentials and may incur charges.

Streaming lets you use an answer before it is complete. It must not make a
partial answer indistinguishable from a completed one.

The proposed R API keeps one ordinary stream contract and gives a live “turn”
one meaning: a view over events that have not yet been collected. Sending
input stays a separate action.

```r
library(lm15)
```

## Display events; keep the response

```r
client <- fake_lm("Hello there.")
req <- request("demo-model", message_user("Say hello."))

answer <- stream(client, req, on_event = function(event) {
  if (event$type == "delta" && event$delta$type == "text") {
    cat(event$delta$text)
  }
})

response_text(answer)
answer$finish_reason
```

The fake client supplies a scripted response. Its event sequence teaches the
interface, not the way a provider would divide the text into chunks.

A **delta** is a change to a content part. The callback receives canonical
start, delta, end and error events. It runs on the R thread. The return value
is the assembled response, including content and metadata that the callback
might not have displayed.

Do not construct your own “response” by concatenating displayed text alone.
That would lose tool calls, media, usage or continuation state. Keep callbacks
small; a slow callback also slows consumption of the stream.

## State the budget at the operation boundary

```r
client <- new_lm("openai", credential = credential_env("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
req <- request("gpt-4.1-mini", message_user("Explain the idea briefly."))

answer <- stream(
  client,
  req,
  on_event = function(event) {
    if (event$type == "delta" && event$delta$type == "text") cat(event$delta$text)
  },
  control = request_control(timeout = 30, max_response_bytes = 8 * 1024^2)
)
```

This is an ordinary completion stream, with an elapsed operation budget.
Preparation and callbacks count toward it. Built-in transport steps receive
the remaining time, rather than starting a fresh full timeout after each step.
Custom callbacks must cooperate; arbitrary R code cannot be safely interrupted
at every instant.

A timeout or local cancellation does not prove that the provider stopped
work or billing. lm15 does not reconnect and replay an ambiguous request to
make the stream look uninterrupted.

## Partial content stays partial

When handling a truncated stream, choose an explicit policy:

```r
attempt <- tryCatch(
  stream(client, req, on_event = function(event) invisible(NULL)),
  StreamAssemblyError = identity
)

if (inherits(attempt, "StreamAssemblyError")) {
  partial <- attempt$partial
  # Inspect or display partial progress; do not store it as completed work.
} else {
  answer <- attempt
}
```

This block describes handling an error, not a claimed example of provider
failure. The existing error class/code remain part of the shared family.
The partial value is useful evidence; it is not a successful short response.

For a consumer test with known data, `response_to_events(response)` and
`materialize_response(events, request)` remain explicit conversions. They
refuse content that cannot be preserved by the delta vocabulary.

## A live connection has a different lifetime

A live session stays open across several exchanges. Its controls describe
connection setup, each idle read, and incoming limits—not a deadline on the
whole conversation.

```r
client <- new_lm("openai", credential = credential_env("OPENAI_API_KEY"))

answer <- with_live(
  client,
  live_config("gpt-realtime"),
  function(session) {
    session$send(live_client_text_event("Hello"))
    view <- turn(session, control = turn_control(timeout = 60))
    result(view)
  },
  control = live_control(read_timeout = 30)
)
```

`with_live()` opens the session, calls the supplied R function, returns its
value, and always attempts local cleanup. It does not send a greeting for you.
Cleanup failure produces a redacted warning rather than replacing a primary
error or retrying the operation.

The explicit alternative uses the same ownership rules:

```r
session <- live(client, live_config("gpt-realtime"))
tryCatch({
  session$send(live_client_text_event("Hello"))
  answer <- result(turn(session))
}, finally = close(session))
```

The preview uses ordinary callbacks and `close()` methods, not a new
non-standard-evaluation language for connection scopes.

## A turn is a view, not a send-and-collect shortcut

There is only one recommended turn meaning:

```r
read_turn <- function(session) {
  session$send(live_client_text_event("What happens next?"))
  view <- turn(session)

  first_event <- next_event(view)
  partial <- snapshot(view)
  result(view)
}

answer <- with_live(client, live_config("gpt-realtime"), read_turn)
```

The helper supplies an open session for the callback's lifetime. `turn(session)` sends
nothing. Reading a view adds events to its local collection; `snapshot(view)`
returns a value without reading another event.

`result(view)` includes already-read events and collects the remainder until
an ending or a tool call. If the last event you read was a tool call, it does
not read past that call while your application still owes an answer.

A turn result contains text, decoded audio, tool calls, usage, errors, original
events, and `ended_by`. Only `"turn_end"` is successful. `"tool_call"`,
`"interrupted"`, `"error"` and `"incomplete"` remain different outcomes.
A view closed before a boundary can expose its snapshot, but cannot fabricate
a successful result.

The old send-and-collect meaning of `session$turn(content)` is deliberately not
part of this proposed primary API. Keeping both under “turn” would force the
reader to remember two incompatible effects and return shapes.

## Bound collection separately from the connection

```r
read_bounded_turn <- function(session) {
  session$send(live_client_text_event("Explain the next step."))
  view <- turn(
    session,
    control = turn_control(
      timeout = 60,
      max_events = 500L,
      max_bytes = 32 * 1024^2
    )
  )
  result(view)
}

answer <- with_live(client, live_config("gpt-realtime"), read_bounded_turn)
```

The collection clock starts on the first read and includes time between reads.
A per-read timeout can shorten a wait, but cannot extend the view's remaining
budget. The connection can outlive this view.

`close(view)` closes only the view. `close(session)` closes the local connection.
Neither name means “cancel every provider action and reverse its charges”.
For immediate audio playback or long-running conversations, use
`next_event(session)` directly instead of collecting the whole turn.

Usage combines all usage-bearing events field by field. An unreported counter
remains unknown, not zero. Independent audio chunks can be decoded and joined;
incompatible media types are refused rather than silently mixed.

## The browser keeps its own asynchronous shape

The proposed browser constructor uses the same credential terminology, but
credentials must be explicit browser values or functions—not a desktop chain:

```js
const client = new Lm15WebR(webR, {
  provider: "gemini",
  credential: async () => getShortLivedCredential(),
});

const session = await client.live({ model: "gemini-live-preview" });
try {
  await session.send({ type: "text", text: "Hello" });
  for await (const event of session.events()) {
    // Read or render the event deliberately.
    if (event.type === "turn_end") break;
  }
} finally {
  await session.close();
}
```

This JavaScript is also a proposal, not an implemented example. It assumes an
initialized webR worker and does not define an application login policy.

Browser restrictions stay visible: required custom WebSocket headers need an
explicit connector or server-side client. No desktop credential files or
metadata services appear magically in the browser. JSON-text methods remain
the exact-number path when JavaScript objects cannot preserve numeric tokens.
